title: Anarchism

cards.b:
Anarchism says that the state is both unnecessary and harmful, and that people can live well through voluntary cooperation. The word comes from the Greek anarkhos, 'without a ruler'.

It is often misread as chaos or bomb-throwing. In theory it is a serious critique of authority. Paper I asks about it in the ideologies unit, usually with Proudhon, Bakunin and Kropotkin.
All anarchists reject the state. They differ on property and on methods.

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, What is Property? (1840), gave the famous answer 'property is theft'. He meant property that lets owners exploit others' labour. He wanted small producers, mutual banks and fair exchange, and a federation of communes.

He was the first to call himself an anarchist. Marx attacked him in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847).

Mikhail Bakunin (1814-76) fought Marx inside the First International. His charge: Marx's 'dictatorship of the proletariat' would only make a new ruling class of party bureaucrats.

He wanted immediate abolition of the state and collective ownership of production. He believed in spontaneous revolt by peasants and workers. Many see his warning as correct about Soviet Russia.

Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid (1902), answered the social Darwinists. Nature, he argued, shows cooperation as much as competition, so human society can run on mutual aid without coercion.

He favoured anarcho-communism: free communes, 'from each according to ability, to each according to need'.
Left anarchists want a stateless, egalitarian society. Anarcho-capitalists want the state replaced by the market. Nozick's minimal state is not anarchism, but he starts from the anarchist question.

Critics raise several objections.

  • Without a state, who stops the strong preying on the weak? Hobbes's problem.
  • Is it utopian? Human nature may not be so cooperative.
  • Big problems like pollution and trade need coordination.
  • Small stateless experiments (Spain 1936-39) were crushed by stronger armies.

Defenders reply that states themselves are the greatest source of war and violence.

Both seek a classless, stateless society. The split is over the path. Marxists use the state (dictatorship of the proletariat) and let it 'wither away'. Anarchists say that a state, once built, never withers.

Link this to Lenin's State and Revolution (1917) and to later critiques of bureaucratic socialism.

Gandhi called his ideal Ram Rajya and 'enlightened anarchy': a society of self-governing villages in 'oceanic circles', where state power is minimal. He said that the best government is the one that governs least.

Differences: Gandhi insisted on non-violence and moral discipline, and he accepted the state as a necessary evil for now. Vinoba Bhave's Sarvodaya and J.P. Narayan's partyless democracy carry the same strand.

"Compare anarchism and Marxism on the state."
"Examine Gandhi's ideas as a form of philosophical anarchism."
"Critically evaluate Kropotkin's idea of mutual aid."

Structure: define, state critique, three thinkers, varieties, link with Marxism, criticism, Gandhi.

quiz.q: Bakunin feared that Marx's plan would produce…
quiz.w: A new class of party rulers.

quiz.q: The first thinker to call himself an anarchist was…

quiz.w: Stirner, The Ego and Its Own (1844).
From each according to ability, to each according to need.

quiz.q: Marxists differ from anarchists mainly on…
o: The path: use the state first
quiz.w: Marxists use the state before it withers.

quiz.q: The standard objection to anarchism is…
o: Strong may dominate the weak without a state

quiz.q: State and Revolution (1917), on the withering away of the state, is by…
quiz.w: Lenin, who kept a transitional workers' state.
